final_answer:
ATTORNEY-CLIENT PRIVILEGED - PREPARED AT THE DIRECTION OF THE AUDIT COMMITTEE

MEMORANDUM to the Audit Committee (L. Fong, Chair; R. Castellano; D. Okwu), from the Office of the Chief Legal Officer. Re: fiduciary standards and process for the proposed $47.5M acquisition of Apex Surgical Supply, LLC (requested April 11, 2025; due April 25, 2025).
Caveats. Law is stated as researched in Oct. 2026, including the March 2025 amendments to 8 Del. C. 144 and Rutledge v. Clearway Energy Group (Del. Feb. 27, 2026), which upheld them. I could not open the Code; statutory descriptions rest on law-firm summaries and must be confirmed against the text. This office reports to management and administers the Article XII register that missed the MSA, so outside counsel should independently verify this memo. Record inconsistencies are listed at the end.

1. SHORT ANSWERS
(a) No approval has occurred, so no review standard yet attaches. But the current process (no committee, no independent advisors, interested Chairman presenting and presiding) would not withstand scrutiny if the deal were signed on it. It is remediable now.
(b) Dr. Whitfield is on both sides: his children's trust takes about $29.45M of the $47.5M, plus a guarantee release and an employment contract for his brother-in-law. At 5.4% of VHS stock he is not a statutory controller on these documents, so the interested-director safe harbor of 144(a) and common-law fairness govern. Actual-control facts are untested; build the process to satisfy the controller standard of 144(b) as well.
(c) Form a special committee of disinterested directors with independent counsel and an independent financial advisor, then consider a disinterested-stockholder vote. Do not sign; do not let June 15 drive the timetable.
(d) Ridgeline's work cannot support approval.
(e) The MSA was never approved under Article XII and the April 1 proxy statement appears inaccurate. Address both first.

2. STANDARD OF REVIEW
Common law (binding Delaware Supreme Court authority). A director on both sides of a transaction invites entire fairness (fair dealing and fair price), burden on defendants (Weinberger v. UOP, 457 A.2d 701 (Del. 1983); Kahn v. Lynch, 638 A.2d 1110 (Del. 1994)). Disinterested approval can shift the burden or restore business judgment review. Old 144 only prevented voidness; it did not displace fiduciary review (Benihana of Tokyo v. Benihana, 906 A.2d 114 (Del. 2006)).
Statute (controlling). Under amended 144(a), an interested-director transaction is not subject to equitable relief or damages if approved in good faith and without gross negligence by (i) a fully informed majority of disinterested directors, or, if a majority of the board is not disinterested, a committee of at least two disinterested directors, or (ii) a fully informed, uncoerced majority of disinterested stockholders. For listed companies, a director whom the board determines meets exchange independence criteria is presumed disinterested, rebuttable only by substantial and particularized facts of a material interest or relationship. Under 144(b), a controlling-stockholder transaction is protected by a committee of at least two disinterested directors with authority to negotiate and reject, or by a disinterested stockholder vote (both for going-private deals). 144(e) defines a controlling stockholder as one with majority voting power, the right to elect a majority of the board, or (as summarized) at least one-third of the vote plus managerial authority.
Application. Dr. Whitfield's 5.4% is far below those thresholds. Common-law "actual control" is fact-intensive (In re Tesla Motors, Inc. S'holder Litig. (Del. Ch. 2018) (22.1% holder pleaded as controller)), and his director seat since 2015, chairmanship since 2018 and agenda control warrant inquiry into his influence over nominations and management. His economics are lopsided: the trust receives 62% of any overpayment while his own VHS shares bear about 5.4%. The safe harbors help only if approvers are genuinely disinterested, informed and uninfluenced; Kahn v. Tremont Corp., 694 A.2d 422 (Del. 1997), found a committee wanting where it deferred to the conflicted party on advisors. 
Exculpation. Certificate Art. VIII preserves liability for loyalty breaches and improper personal benefit.


3. PROCESS DEFICIENCIES
1. Dr. Whitfield authored and distributed the Transaction Overview, presented, fielded all questions and presided throughout; no recusal request, no executive session (Minutes, Part VI). His stated recusal covers only the "final Board vote." This is a real fair-dealing deficiency in substance, but it has no legal effect until the Board or a committee acts; it will be weighed against the later process if he stays involved. The Overview called Ridgeline "independent" and said it "confirms the fairness" of the price; Ridgeline disclaims a fairness opinion.
2. Management worked the deal from February 20 (CEO to CLO) and retained Ridgeline March 3; directors learned April 4. The draft term sheet already fixes price, structure, Granville terms and Dr. Whitfield as Sellers' Representative, so management (reporting to a Board he chairs) set the anchor.
3. No committee and no independent counsel. The Overview proposes existing Audit Committee review and Hargrove & Pemberton, the regular company counsel, "at the Board's direction." No counsel was engaged after Mr. Castellano asked.
4. Article XII requires Audit Committee approval (12.3) and, above $5M, majority approval of disinterested directors (12.5). The Trust is a Related Person entity (12.2(a)(v)). Mr. Granville is not an "immediate family member" (brother-in-law), but his employment is part of the transaction.
5. The April 1 proxy statement says no currently proposed related transactions beyond those described, although this deal was in progress; assess Item 404(a) and Rule 14a-9 exposure.

4. RIDGELINE
Not reliable or independent for committee purposes.
- Engaged by the CFO for management, for "senior management" use only (Letter Section 6); no committee role; fairness opinion only if management requests.
- Fees: $350,000 flat plus $1,200,000 payable only on closing, 77% contingent. Delaware courts scrutinize success fees (El Paso, 41 A.3d 432 (Del. Ch. 2012); Del Monte, 25 A.3d 813 (Del. Ch. 2011)). Ridgeline also advised VHS on three prior deals.
- No verification: the $2.8M of adjustments (31% of adjusted EBITDA) came from Apex management (Mr. Granville) and were not verified. On reported EBITDA of $6.1M the price is about 7.8x, above the whole 4.5x-5.8x range.
- Weak adjustments: the $1.2M lease addback assumes a rent reduction nothing in the term sheet delivers, and lessor Lone Star Properties LP has not been checked for Whitfield ties; the $0.3M owner-compensation addback sits oddly with Mr. Granville's $375,000 plus up to 40% bonus post-closing; $1.3M of litigation and consulting addbacks are unverified.
- The DCF does not reconcile. Using Ridgeline's stated cash flows ($5.8M to $7.9M), 11.5% WACC and 2.5% terminal growth, I compute enterprise value of about $77M (about $25M cash flows plus $52M terminal value), not $46.3M. The "corroboration" cannot be relied on.
- The comparables appendix says names are "used for illustrative purposes"; identities and sources must be confirmed.
- Apex's earnings include $4.7M sold to VHS about 8-12% above market (Internal Audit IA-2025-007, preliminary, 25 SKUs; about $470,000 excess in FY2024). At 5.34x that is roughly $2.5M of price for profit that vanishes on consolidation. Ridgeline does not address it.
- The price is called enterprise value, but Apex carries about $4.1M of debt and the term sheet has no debt-free mechanism; adding it implies about $51.6M, or 5.8x.
Recommendation: the committee retains its own advisor on non-contingent fees, obtains a fairness opinion, and treats Ridgeline as management input.

5. DIRECTOR INDEPENDENCE
Independent per minutes and proxy: Fong, Okwu, Castellano, Rivera, Chen, Pittman. Not independent: Whitfield, Park (CEO reporting to the Chairman-led Board), and Cross (status unstated; treat as non-independent pending review).
Mr. Rivera. About $2M of Whitfield donations over five years to a foundation on whose advisory board he sits, plus his "saw no issues" comment and push for speed. Delaware weighs the totality of personal and financial ties (Delaware County Employees Ret. Fund v. Sanchez, 124 A.3d 1017 (Del. 2015)). Charitable ties alone often do not defeat independence, but exclusion costs little: do not seat him on the committee. He may vote with the Board only after a documented independence determination that considers this relationship; the 144(a) majority does not need him.
Committee candidates: Fong, Castellano, Okwu, with Chen and Pittman as alternates, each cleared by a fresh questionnaire on ties to Whitfield, the Trust, Apex, Granville, Lone Star, Ridgeline and Hargrove. Three members suffice (144 requires two). Their 2019-2024 oversight of an unapproved MSA is a caution, not a disqualifier (Caremark, 698 A.2d 959 (Del. Ch. 1996); Marchand v. Barnhill, 212 A.3d 805 (Del. 2019)); outside counsel should evaluate it.

6. THE MSA AND GOVERNANCE HISTORY
- Internal Audit found no Committee or Board approval of the September 1, 2019 MSA or any annual renewal despite 12.3(a) and (e), with cumulative purchases estimated above $20M (unverified). Bylaw 12.6 says non-compliance does not void a contract but requires prompt ratification review. No approval means no safe harbor; exposure includes a derivative overpayment claim, subject to limitations (by analogy 10 Del. C. 8106, three years) and tolling defenses I have not researched.
- Relevance: a Whitfield-affiliated dealing escaped review for five years, which a plaintiff would cite to show the Company's controls and the current process cannot be trusted, and which supports price protection (indemnity or reduction) for overpayment.
- Renewal falls around September 1, 2025; 12.3(a) bars continuation without approval. Complete a full pricing review and ratify, renegotiate or terminate before then.
- Proxy: "arm's length" and "competitive" lack benchmarking, and the Committee annual-review statement is inaccurate for the MSA. Counsel should assess corrective disclosure before the annual meeting; a stockholder vote cannot be "fully informed" on inaccurate disclosure.

7. RECOMMENDATIONS, IN SEQUENCE
1. Now: instruct management not to sign the term sheet or exclusivity and to act only at the Committee's direction; preserve documents.
2. Board resolution, Dr. Whitfield absent: form a special committee (Fong, Castellano, Okwu) with express power to review, negotiate, reject and consider alternatives, retain advisors at Company expense, and with the Board agreeing not to approve without its favorable recommendation. Record the Board's disinterestedness determinations.
3. Dr. Whitfield steps aside as Chair for this matter (an independent director presides), is excluded from deliberations and privileged materials, and deals with VHS only through the Committee, with his own advisors. Management acts under Committee direction.
4. Committee selects independent counsel (Hargrove only if it has no conflict after disclosure; it is current company counsel advising management) and an independent financial advisor.
5. Re-diligence: quality-of-earnings review of adjustments, Lone Star, MSA pricing, customer concentration, debt-free mechanics. Renegotiate price; strip Dr. Whitfield's control as Sellers' Representative over earnout and indemnity (term sheet Section 16); make indemnity joint and secured; revise the all-or-nothing revenue earnout, which Mr. Granville will manage and which could count VHS purchases.
6. Treat the Granville agreement, guarantee release and guarantee indemnity as conflict items for Committee approval.
7. Resolve MSA ratification and proxy disclosure.
8. Upon a Committee recommendation and fairness opinion, the Board votes with only disinterested directors (12.5; 144(a)). Add a conditional majority-of-disinterested-stockholders vote for a second layer; not legally required on current facts.

8. LITIGATION RISK
Current process: high. Entire fairness likely; fair dealing weak on this record; price support unreliable; injunction or damages claims plausible, including a loyalty claim against Dr. Whitfield outside Art. VIII, and books-and-records demands (narrowed in 2025). The 144 safe harbor is unavailable because no disinterested approval exists.
Remediated process: low to moderate. With real committee authority, independent advisors, accurate disclosure and a disinterested vote, the safe harbors should apply and plaintiffs must attack disinterestedness, information or good faith.
Listing rules: Nasdaq Rule 5630 requires independent related-party review; Rule 5635(a)(2) vote does not appear triggered (about $8.5M stock, roughly 0.25% of shares, my estimate). Verify.
Record inconsistencies: Ridgeline's letter is addressed to CFO Kevin Hartwell but the minutes name Karen Holloway as CFO (she also signs as Director of Internal Audit); Ridgeline's address and phone differ between documents; Ms. Fong may have received the April 2 audit report before April 4.
